headline: Up to 100% basic pay hike proposed for govt employees under 9th Pay Scale
summary: A high-level secretaries' committee has recommended the increase, which is expected to be implemented in two phases, starting with basic salary in the first year.
details: A high-level secretaries’ committee has recommended increasing the basic salaries of government employees in grades one to 20 by up to 100 percent. This recommendation comes from an e-book titled “180 Days of the People’s Government”, published by the Prime Minister’s Office.
The new pay scale is set to be rolled out in two phases. The basic salary component will be implemented in the first year, with house rent and other allowances following in the second year.

The report noted a substantial allocation of Tk 89,836 crore for salaries and allowances in the 2026-27 fiscal year budget. Including pensions and gratuities, the total allocation surpasses Tk 1.41 lakh crore.

Meanwhile, a seven-member cabinet committee met recently to review the salary structure for judiciary employees. Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury stated that the government plans to officially announce the new pay scale this year.

The 9th National Pay Commission, formed on July 27, 2025, submitted its report on January 21 this year. This panel recommended a 100-140 percent increase in total pay and allowances, retaining the existing 20 grades.

Subsequently, a 10-member secretaries’ committee was formed on April 21, headed by Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Gani. Their mandate was to recommend an implementation strategy for the proposed new pay structure.

headline_marked: [[Uncertainty looms over LNG cargo delivery]] as industries still struggle with gas shortages
headline: Uncertainty looms over LNG cargo delivery as industries still struggle with gas shortages
summary: Bangladesh's gas supply has improved, with more diverted to power plants, but industries still face low pressure. The delivery of several crucial LNG cargoes is now uncertain, prolonging the struggle for factories.
details: Bangladesh's gas supply has improved from severe shortages last week, but industries are yet to see a meaningful recovery. A larger share of the limited supply is now being diverted to power plants.
Total gas availability has risen to around 2,420 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd), up from below 300 mmcfd on August 13, against a national demand of approximately 3,800 mmcfd.

Power plants now receive around 930 mmcfd of gas, an increase from 700 mmcfd last week. This has allowed gas-fired plants to generate up to 5,300 megawatts (MW) of electricity, easing the power crisis.

Despite improved electricity supply, many factories have found limited relief. Gas pressure at industrial units remains well below normal in several areas, forcing factories to operate at reduced capacity or keep machinery idle.

For industries dependent on gas-fired boilers, there is often no practical substitute for the fuel. Petrobangla officials indicate that the immediate constraint is now the availability of LNG itself, not just terminal conditions.

Excelerate Energy has confirmed its LNG terminal at Moheshkhali is technically fit for full operation, but faces issues related to LNG supply. The government had anticipated the shortage and planned to procure eight LNG cargoes via Direct Procurement Method (DPM).

At least four of these DPM cargoes were expected to arrive this month, including one this week. However, officials report that the delivery of these cargoes has become uncertain due to a lack of updates from suppliers.

Consequently, state-run Rupantarita Prakritik Gas Company Ltd (RPGCL) floated a tender for five short-term LNG cargoes. Bidders agreed to supply only one of three cargoes requested for August and one of two for early next month.

With only one cargo confirmed for August, expected on the 23rd or 24th, there is little chance of a notable increase in LNG supply before then or the following week. The DPM cargoes were to be procured from international companies outside Petrobangla's enlisted list.

Major industrial groups like Meghna Group and BSRM report only partial recovery. Meghna Group's 57 factories, previously shut, now have gas supply at 60% of normal pressure, allowing limited production but not full capacity.

BSRM's factories are operating at around 50% of normal gas pressure, impacting all 10 of its major units. Ananta Group's four factories in Gazipur, employing approximately 18,000 workers, also face a worsening gas situation.
